title: Replicant Data — November 4, 2026
lead: From billiards and tabletop games to humanoids: how machines test and acquire new abilities.

news.title: A robot calibrates a physical simulator by choosing its own experiments
news.summary: Researchers introduced CUE, which tests physical interactions and updates the physics in a simulated scene. In billiards experiments they report a 72 percent reduction in ball-position prediction error across 25 simulated settings with hidden physical properties.
news.details: Given a high-level instruction, CUE observes the surroundings, proposes parameters for its physical simulation and predicts how objects will move. It then compares the prediction with the observed result and selects the next experiment where the model is least accurate. This is active calibration: the machine takes measurements through action instead of fitting everything from an existing fixed dataset. The paper describes a real-to-simulation-to-real loop in which the system can proceed without a human manually resetting the scene after each test.

Asking an informative question through physical action is the central departure from learning only from finished videos.

They also describe an experiment on a real pool table. This figure concerns prediction error for the tested dynamics; it is not a success rate for arbitrary robotic work. news.body:
A picture of a pool table shows where the balls are but not how quickly they will slow down on the felt. A robot planning its next move needs to estimate friction and how much speed remains after a collision. Researchers led by Xilun Zhang and Marco Pavone presented CUE on November 2, short for Calibration Using Exploration. Rather than merely watch recordings, the system chooses real interactions that reveal physical properties missing from its virtual representation of the scene.

Given a high-level instruction, CUE observes the surroundings, proposes parameters for its physical simulation and predicts how objects will move. It then compares the prediction with the observed result and selects the next experiment where the model is least accurate. This is active calibration: the machine takes measurements through action instead of fitting everything from an existing fixed dataset. The paper describes a real-to-simulation-to-real loop in which the system can proceed without a human manually resetting the scene after each test.

Across 25 simulated hidden-physics conditions, the authors report reducing held-out billiard-ball position error by 72 percent against the strongest baseline. They also describe an experiment on a real pool table. This figure concerns prediction error for the tested dynamics; it is not a success rate for arbitrary robotic work. The paper does not establish an equivalent improvement for cloth, irregular packaging or complicated household objects. The evidence is an author-reported experimental study rather than independent replication.

A person trying an unfamiliar pool table may take a few shots to discover how the balls move. Here the robot does not acquire human intuition; it chooses a test, checks where its calculation went wrong and changes the underlying parameters. Asking an informative question through physical action is the central departure from learning only from finished videos.

news.title: A sub-$2,500 open tabletop arena for competing robots
news.summary: ETH Zurich researchers released KlaskTron, a tabletop system in which two robotic mechanisms learn competitive play. The authors estimate hardware at under 2,500 US dollars and report transferring simulated control to the physical apparatus without additional training.
news.details: Both mechanisms use CoreXY gantry arrangements and brushless motors. The team built a digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, a simulation environment used in robot development, and trained a model of how the motors respond to commands. They report transferring the resulting control policy from simulation to the real tabletop setup without further on-hardware training. Hardware drawings, a bill of materials, assembly instructions, control code and experiment configurations are publicly available. These resources make it possible for other laboratories to scrutinize more than a demonstration video.

news.engineering_impact: The opponent keeps changing its plan, so repeating one memorized movement cannot reliably win. This makes the little board a useful place to watch how an algorithm responds to something unexpected. Unlike many polished demonstrations, the design and software are accessible for closer inspection.
news.limitations: Competition differs from following a fixed movement script because the opponent changes the conditions at every turn. The authors observed behaviors responding to an adversary, but the paper does not guarantee stable play on any independently assembled copy. Precise construction and actuator calibration still matter. Nor does success on a tabletop establish that large humanoids can coordinate safely among people. The practical research contribution is a relatively affordable physical platform on which claims about policy transfer and interaction can be tested.

news.body:
Studying how two learning machines respond to each other is difficult when experiments depend on expensive full-size robots. ETH Zurich researchers proposed a smaller alternative: KlaskTron, a tabletop testbed inspired by the game KLASK. Two controlled mechanisms compete across a board and must respond to the other side's changing actions. The paper appeared on November 2, with the researchers estimating component cost below 2,500 US dollars. The system is primarily a repeatable environment for experiments in multi-agent robot learning, not a product announcement for a commercial arcade game.

Both mechanisms use CoreXY gantry arrangements and brushless motors. The team built a digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, a simulation environment used in robot development, and trained a model of how the motors respond to commands. They report transferring the resulting control policy from simulation to the real tabletop setup without further on-hardware training. Hardware drawings, a bill of materials, assembly instructions, control code and experiment configurations are publicly available. These resources make it possible for other laboratories to scrutinize more than a demonstration video.

Competition differs from following a fixed movement script because the opponent changes the conditions at every turn. The authors observed behaviors responding to an adversary, but the paper does not guarantee stable play on any independently assembled copy. Precise construction and actuator calibration still matter. Nor does success on a tabletop establish that large humanoids can coordinate safely among people. The practical research contribution is a relatively affordable physical platform on which claims about policy transfer and interaction can be tested.

news.title: South Korea opens a humanoid training-data facility with twelve robots
news.summary: South Korea's science ministry announced the opening of a specialized humanoid data collection center on November 3. Twelve robots are operating at the facility, with staged access for external research and industry organizations planned from late 2027.
news.details: Twelve humanoids are already operating, and the government intends to expand both the fleet and the set of recorded activities. Human operators guide machines remotely or demonstrate movements that the robots imitate. Opening-day demonstrations included removing items from a refrigerator, handling laundry, arranging a sofa and pressing controls inside a vehicle. The recordings are intended to support future training of robot-control models. The event also featured development work on the domestic KAIROS humanoid. Capturing a supervised demonstration does not mean the system can already perform every demonstration autonomously.
news.technical_novelty: Twelve humanoids are already operating, and the government intends to expand both the fleet and the set of recorded activities. Human operators guide machines remotely or demonstrate movements that the robots imitate. Opening-day demonstrations included removing items from a refrigerator, handling laundry, arranging a sofa and pressing controls inside a vehicle. Capturing a supervised demonstration does not mean the system can already perform every demonstration autonomously.
news.engineering_impact: The word factory is used for the production of movement records rather than metal parts. People guide the machines while computers preserve examples for later training. The most interesting question is not whether a robot reached into a refrigerator at the opening, but whether another robot can eventually learn from that recording.
news.limitations: Universities, institutes and companies are expected to gain access in phases starting in late 2027. The government hopes shared data production will support domestic technology and reduce reliance on foreign sources. Yet the announcement supplies neither comparable task-success measurements for models trained on the new records nor a total number of recorded hours. It verifies the existence of the facility, the twelve operating robots and an access plan. It does not establish that the eventual models will generalize to unfamiliar homes or factories.

news.organization: Ministry of Science and ICT of South Korea
news.body:
Training a humanoid to handle laundry requires more than a photograph of the finished stack. Researchers need examples showing how an arm moves, when a gripper closes, and how the body adjusts while holding something. On November 3 South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT announced a dedicated collection facility at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials, built with the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute. Officials describe it as the country's first specialized facility for producing task data from bipedal humanoids.

Twelve humanoids are already operating, and the government intends to expand both the fleet and the set of recorded activities. Human operators guide machines remotely or demonstrate movements that the robots imitate. Opening-day demonstrations included removing items from a refrigerator, handling laundry, arranging a sofa and pressing controls inside a vehicle. The recordings are intended to support future training of robot-control models. The event also featured development work on the domestic KAIROS humanoid. Capturing a supervised demonstration does not mean the system can already perform every demonstration autonomously.

Universities, institutes and companies are expected to gain access in phases starting in late 2027. The government hopes shared data production will support domestic technology and reduce reliance on foreign sources. Yet the announcement supplies neither comparable task-success measurements for models trained on the new records nor a total number of recorded hours. It verifies the existence of the facility, the twelve operating robots and an access plan. It does not establish that the eventual models will generalize to unfamiliar homes or factories.

The word factory is used for the production of movement records rather than metal parts. People guide the machines while computers preserve examples for later training. The most interesting question is not whether a robot reached into a refrigerator at the opening, but whether another robot can eventually learn from that recording.

news.title: A humanoid chains walking and handling skills learned separately
news.summary: Seoul National University researchers introduced RISE, a framework linking separately recorded examples of locomotion and object handling. They report 87.3 percent mean success in simulation and a 20-percentage-point advantage over a baseline in experiments with a real Unitree G1.
news.details: The architecture shares visual and language processing across several action specialists, with a coordinator deciding which behavior should be active. During training a specialist receives greater responsibility for examples it predicts accurately. Changes in responsibility weights then help signal a transition to another phase of the task. The real robot is a Unitree G1 fitted with two dexterous hands and 43 controllable degrees of freedom. That is an impressive physical configuration, but it does not mean the model can invent arbitrary skills beyond the kinds of demonstrations used for learning.
news.technical_novelty: The architecture shares visual and language processing across several action specialists, with a coordinator deciding which behavior should be active. During training a specialist receives greater responsibility for examples it predicts accurately. Changes in responsibility weights then help signal a transition to another phase of the task. The real robot is a Unitree G1 fitted with two dexterous hands and 43 controllable degrees of freedom. That is an impressive physical configuration, but it does not mean the model can invent arbitrary skills beyond the kinds of demonstrations used for learning.
news.engineering_impact: Imagine walking to a shelf, choosing an object and then bringing it back. Each step may already be known, yet the transition from one kind of movement to another remains difficult for a machine. The idea is to connect trained abilities by choosing the specialist most relevant at that moment. It is sequential switching rather than unconstrained mixing of every possible motion.
news.limitations: For simulated tasks comprising two to four stages, the team reports an 87.3 percent mean success rate against 73.6 percent for its single-expert comparison. On a real G1, the researchers report a 20-percentage-point advantage, with sequences of up to five stages. The university explicitly identifies truly simultaneous locomotion and dexterous manipulation as future work. Watching a robot walk to a table, pick up an object and move again is evidence of sequential skill composition, not proof of unrestricted autonomy in a crowded home.
news.evidence_status: Evidence: performance figures are reported by the university on behalf of the research team; independent replication is not established.
news.body:
A humanoid robot that can walk and a robot that can grasp a bottle do not automatically know when to switch between those two activities. On October 30, Seoul National University described RISE, developed by Professor Songhwai Oh's team. The name means Responsibility-Induced Specialized Experts, referring to several action models that develop distinct roles during training. The system uses independently collected walking and manipulation demonstrations instead of requiring a recording of every complete sequence. The paper was accepted at the IROS 2026 robotics conference.

The architecture shares visual and language processing across several action specialists, with a coordinator deciding which behavior should be active. During training a specialist receives greater responsibility for examples it predicts accurately. Changes in responsibility weights then help signal a transition to another phase of the task. The real robot is a Unitree G1 fitted with two dexterous hands and 43 controllable degrees of freedom. That is an impressive physical configuration, but it does not mean the model can invent arbitrary skills beyond the kinds of demonstrations used for learning.

For simulated tasks comprising two to four stages, the team reports an 87.3 percent mean success rate against 73.6 percent for its single-expert comparison. On a real G1, the researchers report a 20-percentage-point advantage, with sequences of up to five stages. The university explicitly identifies truly simultaneous locomotion and dexterous manipulation as future work. Watching a robot walk to a table, pick up an object and move again is evidence of sequential skill composition, not proof of unrestricted autonomy in a crowded home.

Imagine walking to a shelf, choosing an object and then bringing it back. Each step may already be known, yet the transition from one kind of movement to another remains difficult for a machine. The idea is to connect trained abilities by choosing the specialist most relevant at that moment. It is sequential switching rather than unconstrained mixing of every possible motion.

news.title: XSTO shows stair-climbing and modular cargo equipment in Shanghai
news.summary: On November 3 XSTO demonstrated stair-climbing and modular cargo-handling equipment at CeMAT Asia 2026 in Shanghai. The company announcement describes the devices but supplies no independent performance comparison or verified long-term industrial operating figures.
news.details: X-Morph uses interchangeable components for level transport, lifting, loading, unloading and moving cargo on stairs. This kind of modularity means physical reconfiguration for different jobs; it does not mean a machine independently understands arbitrary assignments. The company describes its stair-climbing robot as combining autonomous control with heavy-load movement. ET300P2, by contrast, responds to an operator and assists a person who remains involved in the task. Autonomous operation, remotely guided movement and motorized human assistance imply very different staffing and risk requirements.
news.technical_novelty: X-Morph uses interchangeable components for level transport, lifting, loading, unloading and moving cargo on stairs. This kind of modularity means physical reconfiguration for different jobs; it does not mean a machine independently understands arbitrary assignments. The company describes its stair-climbing robot as combining autonomous control with heavy-load movement. ET300P2, by contrast, responds to an operator and assists a person who remains involved in the task. Autonomous operation, remotely guided movement and motorized human assistance imply very different staffing and risk requirements.
news.engineering_impact: Modularity means exchanging physical components to suit a task, not a robot inventing a new way to carry everything. More striking is the difference between equipment that helps a human and equipment described as autonomous. Both may move a load, yet who makes decisions and accepts risk is not the same.
news.limitations: XSTO reports visitor interest and discussions about potential partnerships at the trade show. Its announcement does not provide standardized payload results across different stair geometries, failure statistics, operating speeds or ownership costs. A demonstration stand can show how equipment is built and prompt useful questions from customers, but it cannot replace trials on the intended building's stairs with representative loads. The exhibition runs through November 6; that is the duration of a display rather than a verified start date for a commercial deployment.
news.evidence_status: Evidence: the manufacturer describes a demonstration, without published independent performance tests.
news.body:
The hardest part of delivering a heavy load often begins where a smooth floor ends: at a staircase, narrow landing or vehicle loading edge. On November 3 XSTO announced a display of equipment for such routes at CeMAT Asia 2026 in Shanghai. The lineup includes a stair-climbing robot with intelligent control, modular X-Morph transport platforms, an ET300P2 motorized cart operated through motion-sensitive controls and a compact EzStep stair-climbing cart. This is a manufacturer's exhibition announcement, not an independent test report.

X-Morph uses interchangeable components for level transport, lifting, loading, unloading and moving cargo on stairs. This kind of modularity means physical reconfiguration for different jobs; it does not mean a machine independently understands arbitrary assignments. The company describes its stair-climbing robot as combining autonomous control with heavy-load movement. ET300P2, by contrast, responds to an operator and assists a person who remains involved in the task. Autonomous operation, remotely guided movement and motorized human assistance imply very different staffing and risk requirements.

XSTO reports visitor interest and discussions about potential partnerships at the trade show. Its announcement does not provide standardized payload results across different stair geometries, failure statistics, operating speeds or ownership costs. A demonstration stand can show how equipment is built and prompt useful questions from customers, but it cannot replace trials on the intended building's stairs with representative loads. The exhibition runs through November 6; that is the duration of a display rather than a verified start date for a commercial deployment.

More striking is the difference between equipment that helps a human and equipment described as autonomous. Both may move a load, yet who makes decisions and accepts risk is not the same.

technology_signal.title: Robots learn from trials, games and human examples
technology_signal.summary: This edition follows machines testing physical assumptions, responding to opponents and combining separately learned tasks.
technology_signal.implications: A compelling demonstration is most informative when the verified result remains separate from what is still unknown.
